title: “CARRY EACH OTHER’S BURDENS” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MANY CHRISTIANS THINK IT MEANS
paragraphs: “CARRY EACH OTHER’S BURDENS” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MANY CHRISTIANS THINK IT MEANS
The frightening truth about Galatians 6:2 is that the person God sends you to carry may be messy, ashamed, exhausted, difficult—and one day, that person may be you.
There are some Bible verses we love putting on beautiful backgrounds because the words sound comforting from a distance.
“Carry each other’s burdens.”
It sounds warm.
Safe.
Almost sentimental.
Until the burden has a name.
Until it calls you late at night.
Until it disappoints you again.
Until somebody confesses something you wish you had never heard.
Until the marriage everyone thought was strong begins collapsing behind closed doors.
Until the believer who used to encourage everybody else admits, “I don’t know how much longer I can keep doing this.”
Until the person needing help is the same person who hurt you.
And suddenly Galatians 6:2 is no longer something embroidered onto a Christian wall hanging.
It becomes costly.
“Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” — Galatians 6:2, KJV
Paul originally wrote:
Ἀλλήλων τὰ βάρη βαστάζετε, καὶ οὕτως ἀναπληρώσετε τὸν νόμον τοῦ Χριστοῦ.
Allēlōn ta barē bastazete, kai houtōs anaplērōsete ton nomon tou Christou.
“Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.”
That word translated “burdens” is βάρη — barē, from βάρος — baros.
It speaks of weight.
Heaviness.
Something pressing down.
And the command βαστάζετε — bastazete carries the idea of bearing, carrying, taking up, or supporting a weight.
Paul is not describing Christians standing at a comfortable distance shouting encouragement toward wounded people.
He is describing believers getting underneath weight that is crushing someone else.
But here is what makes this passage even more uncomfortable.
We often quote Galatians 6:2 without Galatians 6:1.
And verse 1 changes the atmosphere completely.
“Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.” — Galatians 6:1, KJV
The Greek word translated “restore” is καταρτίζετε — katartizete, from καταρτίζω — katartizō.
It carries the sense of restoring, repairing, putting something into proper condition.
Paul is talking about restoration.
Not humiliation.
Not gossip disguised as a prayer request.
Not collecting somebody’s failure as evidence that you were spiritually superior all along.
Restoration.
And notice how he says it must happen:
ἐν πνεύματι πραΰτητος — en pneumati prautētos.
“In a spirit of gentleness.”
Why?
Because while you are helping restore the fallen person, Paul tells you to watch yourself.
“Considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.”
In other words:
Be careful how proudly you look at somebody lying in the dirt.
You are made of dust too.
That changes everything.
Because carrying another believer’s burden is not standing above them saying, “How could you?”
Sometimes it is kneeling beside them and whispering:
“Brother, get up.”
“Sister, come home.”
“What happened was sin, but your sin does not have to write the final chapter of your life.”
“Jesus is still calling you.”
There is a difference between excusing sin and restoring a sinner.
Biblical grace never requires pretending darkness is light.
Jesus did not have to redefine sin in order to rescue sinners from it.
The Gospel is far more beautiful than that.
Sin can be named honestly.
Repentance can be required urgently.
Consequences can remain painfully real.
And grace can still say:
“Come home.”
That is the scandal.
That is the grace.
Because Christianity was never the story of respectable people saving embarrassing people.
Christianity is the story of sinners being rescued by Jesus Christ.
And perhaps we forget that because we have become very skilled at hiding our own weight.
Someone reading this right now is tired.
Not physically tired.
Soul tired.
You still answer, “I’m good.”
You still go to work.
You still take care of everybody.
You still post the birthday message.
You still respond with the praying-hands emoji.
You may even still attend church.
But there is something you are carrying that almost nobody knows about.
Maybe it is grief.
Maybe debt.
Maybe temptation.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe anger.
Maybe a marriage slowly freezing to death.
Maybe a child who has walked away from God.
Maybe shame from something that happened years ago.
Maybe the exhaustion of being everybody’s strong person.
Maybe you have become frighteningly good at smiling while drowning.
And somewhere along the way, you started believing that needing somebody to help carry your burden meant you were failing spiritually.
Galatians 6 says otherwise.
There are weights God never intended you to carry alone.
But this passage also contains a tension Christians sometimes miss.
Only a few verses later Paul writes:
Wait.
Verse 2 says bear one another’s burdens.
Verse 5 says each person bears his own burden.
Contradiction?
No.
The Greek helps us see the distinction.
Galatians 6:2 uses βάρη — barē, heavy burdens or weights.
Galatians 6:5 uses φορτίον — phortion, a load or responsibility assigned to someone.
The point is not that Christians should take responsibility away from one another.
It is that we should refuse to let one another be crushed by unbearable weight.
Biblical burden-bearing is therefore neither abandonment nor unhealthy rescuing.
You cannot repent for somebody else.
You cannot obey God for somebody else.
You cannot make somebody forgive.
You cannot force somebody to leave an addiction.
You cannot believe the Gospel on somebody else’s behalf.
You cannot become another person's Messiah.
That position is already occupied.
His name is Jesus.
Sometimes loving someone means helping them carry what is crushing them.
Sometimes loving someone means refusing to carry the responsibility God has commanded them to carry themselves.
Both can be love.
That distinction matters because some people have been destroyed trying to “carry someone’s burdens” when what they were actually doing was enabling destructive behavior.
Covering someone’s repeated deception is not necessarily burden-bearing.
Protecting an abuser from accountability is not biblical restoration.
Helping someone avoid every consequence of rebellion is not automatically grace.
Jesus is compassionate, but His compassion never requires us to become accomplices to darkness.
Biblical love “rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth” (1 Corinthians 13:6).
Sometimes love sits beside you while you cry.
Sometimes love pays for groceries.
Sometimes love drives you to counseling.
Sometimes love answers at midnight.
Sometimes love listens without immediately trying to fix everything.
Sometimes love says, “I will walk through this with you.”
And sometimes love looks you in the eyes and says:
“I love you too much to help you destroy yourself.”
Both may be burden-bearing.
Because the goal is not dependency on us.
The goal is restoration in Christ.
And this is where Galatians 6:2 becomes breathtaking.
Paul says that when we bear one another’s burdens, we “fulfil the law of Christ.”
What is this law of Christ?
Jesus told His disciples:
“A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you.” — John 13:34, KJV
Read the last part again.
As I have loved you.
That is the standard.
Not love one another when convenient.
Not love one another when respectable.
Not love one another when the person's struggle photographs well.
“As I have loved you.”
And how did Christ love us?
Look at the cross.
Jesus did not merely sympathize with our burden.
He entered our suffering.
Scripture says of Christ:
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree.” — 1 Peter 2:24, KJV
The Greek verb there is ἀνήνεγκεν — anēnenken.
He bore our sins.
Isaiah had prophesied centuries earlier:
“Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows.” — Isaiah 53:4, KJV
The Hebrew is staggering:
אָכֵן חֳלָיֵנוּ הוּא נָשָׂא וּמַכְאֹבֵינוּ סְבָלָם
Akhen cholayenu hu nasa, umakh’oveinu sevalam.
Surely our griefs He bore, and our sorrows He carried.
There it is.
Before Paul told Christians to carry one another’s burdens, Scripture had already revealed the ultimate Burden-Bearer.
Jesus Christ.
We carry because He carried.
We forgive because we were forgiven.
We restore because He restores.
We show mercy because mercy found us first.
We kneel beside fallen people because Christ came down into our ruin to rescue us.
But we must make an essential distinction.
Jesus carries something for us that no Christian friend ever can.
Our sin.
No pastor can bear its judgment for you.
No spouse can.
No parent can.
No church can.
No ministry can.
No amount of generosity can.
No religious performance can.
At the cross, Jesus did what only the spotless Son of God could do.
He bore sin.
He received judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And He rose again.
So Christianity is not ultimately:
“Carry enough people and God will accept you.”
It is:
“Christ carried what you could never carry, and because you have been loved by Him, go love others.”
That order matters.
Grace first.
Transformation afterward.
The Gospel is not a ladder exhausted sinners climb toward God.
It is the announcement that in Jesus Christ, God came down to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
Maybe that is why this command hurts so much.
Because carrying burdens requires proximity.
You cannot carry something from across the room.
You have to come close.
Close enough to hear the confession.
Close enough to see the tears.
Close enough to discover that the person everyone calls “strong” is barely holding together.
Close enough to realize that behind someone’s anger may be grief.
Behind someone’s silence may be shame.
Behind someone’s addiction may be a person desperately trying to anesthetize pain.
Behind someone’s spiritual coldness may be disappointment they were afraid to admit.
This does not excuse sin.
It reminds us that sinners are human beings, not projects.
And Jesus was remarkably willing to come close.
To lepers.
To tax collectors.
To prostitutes.
To grieving families.
To doubters.
To failures.
To people respectable society preferred to avoid.
Think about Peter.
Peter had promised Jesus:
“Though all men shall be offended because of thee, yet will I never be offended.” — Matthew 26:33, KJV
Hours later, he denied Him.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke tells us something devastating.
“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.” — Luke 22:61, KJV
Imagine that moment.
The eyes of the Man you swore you would never abandon.
And you just abandoned Him.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
If Christianity were merely a religion of scandal, Peter’s story could have ended there.
Failure.
Hypocrisy.
Coward.
Disqualified.
But Jesus was not finished writing.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
Not to pretend the denial never happened.
Jesus brought Peter directly back to the question of love.
“Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?” — John 21:16, KJV
And then:
“Feed my sheep.”
Peter’s failure was real.
But failure did not receive authorship over Peter’s future.
Jesus did.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you need to hear that tonight.
Your worst chapter does not outrank the blood of Christ.
Your shame is not stronger than His mercy.
Your failure is not too complicated for His redemption.
But grace is not Jesus helping you decorate your chains.
Grace breaks them.
Grace calls you out.
Grace calls you home.
Grace tells the truth about your sin while opening the door to forgiveness.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
So perhaps the burden you need help carrying begins with three terrifying words:
“I need help.”
Maybe four:
“Please pray for me.”
Maybe:
“I have been hiding.”
Maybe:
“I messed up.”
Maybe:
“I’m not okay.”
Maybe:
“I need to repent.”
There is no medal in heaven for pretending you were never wounded.
There is no spiritual prize for bleeding privately so everybody can continue believing you are strong.
The body of Christ is supposed to be a body.
When one member suffers, Scripture says the others suffer with it.
That means the church should be one of the few places on earth where confession does not automatically become entertainment.
Where wounded people are not turned into gossip.
Where repentance is celebrated.
Where truth and mercy meet.
Where people can say, “I am struggling,” and somebody answers, “Then you are not walking alone.”
And perhaps there is someone God is placing on your heart right now.
A name.
A face.
Someone you have not checked on.
Someone whose posts became quieter.
Someone who stopped coming around.
Someone who laughs loudly enough that nobody thinks to ask whether they are okay.
Someone who failed publicly.
Someone you quietly judged.
Someone who needs truth, but also needs a hand reaching into the wreckage.
Call them.
Message them.
Pray with them.
Bring food.
Sit quietly.
Help practically.
Point them toward wise pastoral care or professional help when appropriate.
Do not become their savior.
Bring them toward the Savior.
And if you are the one underneath the weight...
Please stop believing the lie that hiding makes you holy.
Bring your sin into the light.
Bring your suffering into community.
Find mature, trustworthy believers.
Ask for prayer.
Seek biblical counsel.
Where necessary, seek qualified professional help.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Set wise boundaries where safety requires them.
And keep walking toward Jesus.
Maybe you cannot carry tomorrow yet.
Then carry today.
And when today is too heavy, let somebody carry part of it with you.
That is not weakness.
That is Galatians 6.

And one day, after Christ has carried you through a season you thought would destroy you, you may discover that the scars you once wanted to hide have become places from which you can recognize another wounded person.
You will hear someone say, “Nobody understands.”
And quietly you will think:
I do.
You will see somebody falling where you once fell.
And instead of throwing a stone, you will remember the hand that reached for you.
That is how grace multiplies.
Not because sin becomes less serious.
Because mercy becomes more astonishing.
You do not have to explain everything publicly.
Those three words are enough.

And if Christ has already carried you through something you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what Jesus did. Your testimony may become the hand God uses to reach someone who thinks there is no road home.
Not because every sentence is easy, but because there may come a night when you forget that Christians were never commanded to suffer alone.

If you want your giving and support to glorify God, let it flow from worship and love rather than pressure: Scripture teaches that Christian giving is to be willing, cheerful, and not compelled (2 Corinthians 9:7).
It is discipleship.
It is helping more people encounter Scripture, conviction, encouragement, repentance, grace, healing, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
But before you leave this article, remember the person whose name entered your mind while reading it.
Do not assume somebody else will call them.
Do not assume somebody else knows.
Do not assume the smile means the weight is light.
And if the person God brought to your mind was you...
Then hear the Gospel again.
You are not being invited to pretend.
You are being invited to Christ.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Receive His mercy.
Let trustworthy believers walk beside you.
Because the church was never supposed to be a showroom for people who never broke.
It is a people gathered around a crucified and risen Savior who knows exactly what crushing weight feels like.
We carry one another because He first carried us.
We restore because He restores.
We forgive because He forgave.
We love because He first loved us.
And perhaps the person barely surviving beneath a burden today will someday become the person God uses to help carry someone else home.
Never be ashamed of the chapter Jesus is still rewriting.
